entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: In English, a *chef* is a professional cook, usually the one in charge of a restaurant kitchen. German *Chef*, the person you report to, is *boss* or *manager*.
entries.usage: *My chef wants the report by Friday* will make Americans picture a cook in a white hat. *Head chef* or *executive chef* runs a kitchen, and the word also appears in *pastry chef* and *TV chef*. For the person above you at work, say *my boss* casually and *my manager* in formal contexts.
examples: The **chef** came out of the kitchen to ask how we liked the fish.
My **boss** is out sick today, so the team meeting is canceled.
My mom loves a TV **chef** who makes every dinner in thirty minutes.

drill.sentence: I'll ask my {{boss}} if I can take Monday off for my brother's wedding.
drill.hint: chef or boss? (the person you report to at work)

mistake.wrong: My chef is on vacation, so I can't get approval until next week.
mistake.right: My boss is on vacation, so I can't get approval until next week.
mistake.why: German *Chef* is *boss* or *manager*; an English *chef* is a cook.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: German *Handy* is a *cell phone*, or just *phone*, in American English. English *handy* is an adjective that means useful and convenient, or good at fixing and building things.
entries.usage: Americans mostly say *phone* or *cell* (*Call me on my cell*); *cell phone* is used when you need to be clear, and *mobile phone* is British. *Handy* is common in speech: *That'll come in handy*, *a handy tool*, *He's handy around the house*. Never use *handy* as a noun.
examples: I left my **cell phone** in the cab, so I can't call anyone.
These little hooks are really **handy** for hanging keys by the door.
My brother-in-law is really **handy**; he built our deck himself.

drill.sentence: Keep a phone charger in your glove box; it'll come in {{handy}} on long road trips.
drill.hint: cell phone or handy? (be useful someday; fixed phrase)

mistake.wrong: Sorry, my handy was on silent.
mistake.right: Sorry, my phone was on silent.
mistake.why: German *Handy* is *phone* or *cell phone*; English *handy* is an adjective meaning useful.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: In English, a *billion* is a thousand million (1,000,000,000), which is German *Milliarde*. A *trillion* is a million million, which is German *Billion*.
entries.usage: This difference causes real errors in reports, news and translations: *drei Billionen Euro* is *three trillion euros*. There is no English word *milliard* in normal use. After a number, *billion* and *trillion* take no plural *-s*: *two billion people*, *$4 trillion*.
examples: The new airport terminal cost about $1.5 **billion**.
The world's population passed eight **billion** in 2022.
A **trillion** seconds adds up to more than 31,000 years.

drill.sentence: Germany's economy produces goods and services worth more than four {{trillion}} euros a year.
drill.hint: billion or trillion? (German *Billionen*)

mistake.wrong: The project cost two milliards dollars.
mistake.right: The project cost two billion dollars.
mistake.why: English uses *billion* for German *Milliarde*, with no plural *-s* after a number.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: German *Rezept* has two English words: a *recipe* tells you how to cook a dish, and a *prescription* is a doctor's written order for medicine.
entries.usage: You *fill* a prescription at a pharmacy, and medicine that needs one is *prescription medicine*; medicine you can buy without one is *over-the-counter*. Doctors *prescribe* drugs, and cooks *follow* a recipe. *A recipe for disaster* is a common figurative phrase.
examples: My grandma's **recipe** for apple pie calls for a pinch of nutmeg.
I need to pick up my **prescription** at the pharmacy before it closes.
Icy roads and tired drivers are a **recipe** for disaster.

drill.sentence: The doctor wrote me a {{prescription}} for antibiotics and told me to take them for ten days.
drill.hint: prescription or recipe? (a doctor's order for medicine)

mistake.wrong: I can't buy these pills without a recipe.
mistake.right: I can't buy these pills without a prescription.
mistake.why: German *Rezept* for medicine is *prescription*; a *recipe* is for cooking.

entries.term: here you go / you're welcome (German bitte)
entries.label: usage trap
entries.meaning: German *bitte* has several English equivalents. When you hand something to someone, say *here you go*; when someone thanks you, say *you're welcome*; *please* is only for requests.
entries.usage: Answering *thank you* with *please* sounds strange in English. Americans also reply to thanks with *sure*, *no problem*, *of course* or *my pleasure*, which is common in hotels and restaurants. *Here you go* is the usual phrase when you hand over food, change or a document; *here you are* is a little more formal.
examples: "Two lattes and a blueberry muffin." "**Here you go**. Have a great day!"
"Thanks for fixing my bike!" "**You're welcome**. It only took a minute."
The pharmacist handed me the bag and said, "**Here you go**. Take one with food."

drill.sentence: "Thank you so much for watering my plants while I was away." "{{You're welcome}}. They were no trouble at all."
drill.hint: the standard reply to thanks; German *bitte* (not *please* or *no problem*)

mistake.wrong: "Thank you for your help!" "Please!"
mistake.right: "Thank you for your help!" "You're welcome!"
mistake.why: German *bitte* after thanks is *you're welcome*; English *please* is only used in requests.

entries.label: usage trap
entries.meaning: German *wenn* can mean both. Use *when* for something you expect to happen, and *if* for something that may or may not happen.
entries.usage: *When I see her, I'll tell her* means you will surely see her; *If I see her, I'll tell her* means you might not. *When* also means *every time* (*When it rains, the basement floods*). Choosing the wrong word can change the tone: *When you're late again, …* assumes you will be late.
examples: **When** we get to the hotel, let's take a nap before dinner.
**If** it rains on Saturday, we'll move the picnic indoors.
Call me **when** you're done at the doctor's, and I'll pick you up.

drill.sentence: {{If}} I ever win the lottery, I'll buy a little house on the beach.
drill.hint: when or if? (it may never happen)

mistake.wrong: When I have time tomorrow, I'll call you, but I'm not sure I will.
mistake.right: If I have time tomorrow, I'll call you, but I'm not sure I will.
mistake.why: German *wenn* covers both; when you are not sure it will happen, English uses *if*.

entries.label: verb pattern
entries.meaning: *Explain* takes the thing explained as its object, and the person comes after *to*: *explain something to someone*. Unlike *tell* or *show*, it never takes the person directly after the verb.
entries.usage: Say *Can you explain this to me?* or *Can you explain to me how it works?*; *explain me* is one of the most common learner errors. With a long object, *to me* usually comes first: *She explained to us why the flight was canceled*. *Describe*, *suggest* and *say* follow the same pattern.
entries.pattern: explain something to someone / explain to someone + wh-clause
examples: Can you **explain** the rules **to me** one more time?
The nurse **explained to us** how to change the bandage.
Let me **explain to you** why we chose this neighborhood.

drill.sentence: Could you {{explain to me}} how the new parking app works?
drill.hint: explain + the person: the correct pattern

mistake.wrong: Can you explain me the difference?
mistake.right: Can you explain the difference to me?
mistake.why: *Explain* never takes the person directly; use *explain something to someone*.

entries.label: verb pattern
entries.meaning: *Discuss* takes a direct object, so no preposition follows it: *discuss the plan*. The noun and similar verbs do take *about*: *a discussion about*, *talk about*.
entries.usage: German *diskutieren über* leads to *discuss about*, a very common error. In speech, *talk about* and *go over* (*Let's go over the budget*) are often more natural than *discuss*. The noun takes *about* or *of*: *a discussion about prices*.
entries.pattern: discuss + object / talk about + object / a discussion about
examples: We need to **discuss** the budget before the end of the month.
My sister and I **discussed** whether to sell our parents' house.
The book club had a long **discussion about** the ending.

drill.sentence: I'd like to {{discuss}} my salary with you at our next one-on-one.
drill.hint: talk over; no preposition after the verb

mistake.wrong: We discussed about the new schedule.
mistake.right: We discussed the new schedule.
mistake.why: *Discuss* takes a direct object; use *about* only after *talk* or the noun *discussion*.

entries.label: preposition
entries.meaning: *For* is followed by a length of time (*for three years*, *for a week*). *Since* is followed by a starting point (*since 2021*, *since Monday*, *since I was a kid*).
entries.usage: German *seit* covers both, which leads to *since three years*. When the situation continues now, both usually go with the present perfect: *I've lived here for three years*. *For* also works with the simple past and the future (*I lived there for a year*), but *since* normally needs a perfect tense (*I've lived here since 2021*).
examples: We've been married **for** twelve years now.
She's worked at the hospital **since** 2019.
The road to the lake has been closed **for** months because of a landslide.

drill.sentence: My parents have lived in that apartment {{for}} almost thirty years.
drill.hint: for or since? (followed by a length of time)

mistake.wrong: I'm learning English since five years.
mistake.right: I've been learning English for five years.
mistake.why: A length of time takes *for*, and something that started in the past and continues now needs the present perfect.

entries.term: I've been here since … (not 'I am here since …')
entries.label: tense
entries.meaning: For a state or action that started in the past and continues now, English uses the present perfect (*I've been*, *I've lived*, *I've known*), not the present tense.
entries.usage: German *Ich bin seit März hier* uses the present, but English needs *I've been here since March*; for ongoing activities, the present perfect progressive is common (*I've been working here since May*). The simple present with *since* is wrong in standard English. Careful with *for*: *I'm here for two weeks* is correct, but it means the whole visit will last two weeks.
examples: **I've been** in Seattle since August, and I still get lost downtown.
**She's known** him since middle school.
**We've had** this car since 2015, and it still runs perfectly.

drill.sentence: {{I've been}} a vegetarian since college, so I'll skip the burgers, thanks.
drill.hint: *I* + the right form of *be* for a state that started in the past and is still true

mistake.wrong: I am here since March.
mistake.right: I've been here since March.
mistake.why: A state that started in the past and continues now needs the present perfect, not the present tense.

entries.label: time expression
entries.meaning: *Ago* comes after a length of time and counts back from now: *two years ago*, *a week ago*. German *vor zwei Jahren* is *two years ago*, not *before two years*.
entries.usage: Use *ago* with the simple past (*I moved here two years ago*), never with the present perfect. *Before* goes with a point in time (*before 2020*, *before lunch*). *Two years before* means two years earlier than another past event (*She had left two years before*).
examples: My grandfather learned to swim **five years ago**, at the age of seventy.
I talked to her just **ten minutes ago**.
The bridge was built **over a century ago**.

drill.sentence: I bought this laptop only {{six months ago}}, and the battery is already dying.
drill.hint: *vor sechs Monaten* in natural English

mistake.wrong: I met him before two years in Berlin.
mistake.right: I met him two years ago in Berlin.
mistake.why: German *vor* + a length of time is *ago*, placed after the time phrase.

entries.label: collocation
entries.meaning: In English, you *take* a photo or a picture with a camera or phone. German *ein Foto machen* does not translate word for word.
entries.usage: *Make a photo* sounds wrong to native speakers. You *take a photo of* someone, *take a selfie*, and *have your photo taken* when someone else does it. *Take a picture* is the most common phrase in American speech, and *snap a photo* is casual.
examples: My dad **takes a picture** of every meal he eats on vacation.
I **took** over two hundred **photos** at the Grand Canyon.
We had our passport **photos taken** at the drugstore.

drill.sentence: Excuse me, would you mind {{taking}} a photo of my friends and me?
drill.hint: make or take? (with *a photo*)

mistake.wrong: Can I make a photo of you?
mistake.right: Can I take a photo of you?
mistake.why: German *ein Foto machen* is *take a photo* in English; *make a photo* is not used.

entries.term: take an exam (not 'make' or 'write an exam')
entries.label: collocation
entries.meaning: In American English, you *take* an exam or a test, and you *pass* it if you succeed. German *eine Prüfung machen* or *schreiben* is *take an exam*.
entries.usage: *Make an exam* sounds wrong; *write an exam* is Canadian and *sit an exam* is British, and both sound odd to most Americans. Teachers *give* exams, and students *take* them. *Pass* always means you succeeded, and *fail* means you didn't.
examples: I'm **taking** my driving **test** next Tuesday, and I'm really nervous.
Did you **pass** your real estate exam?
Students who miss the final can **take** it the following week.

drill.sentence: Most nursing students {{take}} the licensing exam a few weeks after graduation.
drill.hint: make, write or take? (sit for an exam, US)

mistake.wrong: Tomorrow I will write my math exam.
mistake.right: Tomorrow I'll take my math exam.
mistake.why: Americans *take* an exam; German *eine Prüfung schreiben* or *machen* does not translate word for word.

entries.label: collocation
entries.meaning: In English, you *take* a break, a vacation or a day off. German *eine Pause machen* is *take a break*.
entries.usage: *Make a break* is wrong in this sense, and *make a break for it* means *run away*. The same verb works in *take a day off*, *take a nap* and *take a vacation*. In meetings, *Let's take a ten-minute break* is the standard phrase.
examples: You've been studying for hours; why don't you **take a break**?
I'm **taking** Friday **off** to drive to my cousin's wedding.
The kids **took a break** from swimming to eat their sandwiches.

drill.sentence: We've been driving for four hours. Let's stop at the next rest area and {{take}} a break.
drill.hint: make or take? (with *a break*)

mistake.wrong: Let's make a short break.
mistake.right: Let's take a short break.
mistake.why: German *Pause machen* is *take a break*; *make a break* is not used for resting (*make a break for it* means run away).

entries.label: uncountable noun
entries.meaning: *Information* is uncountable in English: it has no plural and does not take *a*. For one item, say *a piece of information*, or more naturally *a detail* or *a fact*.
entries.usage: Use *some information*, *a lot of information*, *more information*, never *informations* or *an information*. The verb is singular: *The information is correct*. *Info* is a casual short form (*Send me the info*).
examples: The hotel website has a lot of useful **information** about parking.
Thanks for the **info**; I'll pass it on to everyone else.
For more **information**, call our office between nine and five.

drill.sentence: The museum's front desk can give you {{information}} about guided tours.
drill.hint: the uncountable noun for facts and details

mistake.wrong: Thank you for all the informations.
mistake.right: Thank you for all the information.
mistake.why: *Information* is uncountable, so it has no plural form.

entries.label: agreement
entries.meaning: *People* is the normal plural of *person*, so it takes a plural verb: *people are*, *people have*, *people say*.
entries.usage: Use *many people* and *a lot of people*, not *much people*. *A people* (plural *peoples*) means a nation or ethnic group (*the peoples of Central Asia*). For one human, say *a person*; *persons* is legal or formal (*no more than four persons*).
examples: **People are** always surprised by how hot it gets here in June.
**People have** been lining up outside the store since 5 a.m.
Most **people** in my building **have** a cat or a dog.

drill.sentence: A lot of {{people are}} still stuck at the airport because of the snowstorm.
drill.hint: the plural word for humans + the right form of *be*

mistake.wrong: The people in this town is very friendly.
mistake.right: The people in this town are very friendly.
mistake.why: *People* is plural, so it takes a plural verb.

entries.label: verb pattern
entries.meaning: In *look forward to*, the word *to* is a preposition, not part of an infinitive, so a noun or an -ing form follows: *look forward to seeing you*.
entries.usage: *I look forward to hearing from you* is a standard, slightly formal email closing; *I'm looking forward to it* is warmer and common in speech. The same rule applies to *be used to*, *object to* and *when it comes to*: *I'm not used to driving on the left*.
examples: We're really **looking forward to** the beach trip in July.
I'm **looking forward to meeting** your parents on Sunday.
The kids are **looking forward to decorating** cookies this weekend.

drill.sentence: I'm really looking forward to {{seeing}} you all at the wedding in June.
drill.hint: *see* in the right form after *look forward to*

mistake.wrong: I look forward to see you next week.
mistake.right: I look forward to seeing you next week.
mistake.why: In *look forward to*, *to* is a preposition, so the verb takes the -ing form.

entries.term: I want you to come (not 'I want that you come')
entries.label: verb pattern
entries.meaning: *Want* is followed by an object and a *to*-infinitive: *I want you to come*. It cannot take a *that*-clause, so German *Ich will, dass du kommst* does not translate word for word.
entries.usage: The same object + *to* pattern works with *would like*, *need*, *ask* and *tell*: *I'd like you to meet my sister*. *Want* and *would like* never take a *that*-clause in English. For a softer request, *I'd like you to…* or *Could you…?* sounds more polite than *I want you to…*.
entries.pattern: want / would like / need + person + to + verb
examples: **I want you to come** to my birthday dinner on Friday.
My mom **wants me to** text her every time I land.
**I'd like you to** meet my roommate, Jess.

drill.sentence: My parents {{want me to}} call them every Sunday, even when I'm busy.
drill.hint: *want* + person + the right verb form (no *that*)

mistake.wrong: I want that you help me with the move.
mistake.right: I want you to help me with the move.
mistake.why: *Want* takes an object and *to* + verb, never a *that*-clause.

entries.label: verb pattern
entries.meaning: *Agree* is a verb, so you say *I agree*, *I don't agree* and *We agreed*. *I am agree* mixes it with German *Ich bin einverstanden*, which uses *be* + adjective.
entries.usage: Use *agree with* a person or opinion, *agree on* a decision (*We agreed on a price*) and *agree to* a request or plan (*She agreed to help*). *I'm in agreement* exists but sounds formal. In speech, *Totally*, *Exactly* and *I couldn't agree more* show strong agreement.
entries.pattern: agree with someone / agree on something / agree to do something
examples: **I agree** with you; the second apartment has a much better kitchen.
We finally **agreed** on a name for the puppy.
She **agreed** to look after our cat while we're away.

drill.sentence: I don't {{agree}} that the beach was too crowded; we found a great spot by the rocks.
drill.hint: have the same opinion (a verb, so no *am*)

mistake.wrong: I am agree with your idea.
mistake.right: I agree with your idea.
mistake.why: *Agree* is a verb, so it needs no *am*; German *einverstanden sein* has no word-for-word equivalent.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: English *gift* means a present, something you give someone. German *Gift* is *poison* in English.
entries.usage: *Gift* is slightly more formal than *present* and common in shops (*gift card*, *gift shop*, *gift wrap*); *a gift for* something is a natural talent (*a gift for languages*). *Poison* is the substance, and *poisonous* describes mushrooms, plants and chemicals. *Toxic* is also common, especially for chemicals.
examples: We bought her a **gift** card because we had no idea what she wanted.
Keep rat **poison** away from children and pets.
He has a real **gift** for telling stories.

drill.sentence: The museum {{gift}} shop sells postcards, mugs and copies of famous paintings.
drill.hint: gift or poison? (as in a present)

mistake.wrong: Be careful, those mushrooms contain gift.
mistake.right: Be careful, those mushrooms are poisonous.
mistake.why: German *Gift* is *poison*; English *gift* means a present.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: German *Konkurrenz* is *competition* (rivalry) or *the competition* (your competitors). English *concurrence* is a rare, formal word for agreement, or for events happening at the same time.
entries.usage: In business, *the competition* means rival companies (*Our prices are lower than the competition's*), and *competitors* are specific rivals. *Competition* is also an event (*a baking competition*). *Concurrence* is rare outside law and formal writing, so never use it for *Konkurrenz*.
examples: There's a lot of **competition** for apartments in this neighborhood.
Our daughter won second place in a state piano **competition**.
The local hardware store survived by offering better service than the **competition**.

drill.sentence: Two new coffee shops opened on our block, so the café downstairs is worried about the {{competition}}.
drill.hint: competition or concurrence? (rival businesses)

mistake.wrong: We have strong concurrence from Asian companies.
mistake.right: We have strong competition from Asian companies.
mistake.why: German *Konkurrenz* is *competition*; English *concurrence* means agreement.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: In the US, a *grade* is the mark a student gets on a test or in a class, such as an A or a B (German *Note*). A *note* in English is a short written message, or a musical tone.
entries.usage: Americans say *get good grades* and *What grade did you get?*; British English uses *mark*. *Grade* also means a school year in the US (*She's in fifth grade*). *Notes* are what you write down in class (*take notes*) or leave for someone (*a note on the fridge*).
examples: She got the best **grades** in her class and a full scholarship to Stanford.
I left a **note** on the door for the delivery driver.
My son's in third **grade** and loves math.

drill.sentence: If you want to get into a good college, your {{grades}} in high school really matter.
drill.hint: grade or note? (the A, B or C on a report card)

mistake.wrong: I got a good note on my chemistry test.
mistake.right: I got a good grade on my chemistry test.
mistake.why: German *Note* is *grade* in American English; a *note* is a short message.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: German *Hochschule* is a university or college. An American *high school* is a secondary school for grades 9 to 12, roughly ages 14 to 18.
entries.usage: Saying you studied at *a high school* in Germany makes Americans think you were a teenager there. Translate *Hochschule* as *university* or *college*, and *Fachhochschule* as *university of applied sciences*. American *high school* matches roughly the last years of German secondary school.
examples: My brother teaches chemistry at a public **high school** in Oregon.
She studied mechanical engineering at a technical **university** in Munich.
We met in **high school** and got married ten years later.

drill.sentence: He earned his engineering degree at a {{university}} of applied sciences in Stuttgart.
drill.hint: high school or university? (German *Hochschule*)

mistake.wrong: I studied computer science at a high school in Germany.
mistake.right: I studied computer science at a university in Germany.
mistake.why: An American *high school* is for teenagers; German *Hochschule* is a *university* or *college*.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: German *meinen* often means *think* or *believe*, as in *Ich meine, dass…*. English *mean* is about intention or meaning: what you are trying to say, or what a word or sign signifies.
entries.usage: Say *I think you're right*, not *I mean you're right*, and ask *What do you think?* for an opinion; *What do you mean?* asks for an explanation. *I mean* at the start of a sentence is a filler that clarifies or softens what you just said (*I mean, it's not terrible*). *Mean to* + verb is *intend to* (*I didn't mean to hurt you*).
examples: When I said the soup was interesting, I didn't **mean** it was bad.
What do you **think** about painting the kitchen yellow?
A red flag on the beach **means** no swimming.

drill.sentence: "Should we take the highway or the back roads?" "I {{think}} the back roads will be faster at this hour."
drill.hint: mean or think? (giving your opinion)

mistake.wrong: What do you mean about the new schedule?
mistake.right: What do you think about the new schedule?
mistake.why: German *meinen* for opinions is *think*; *What do you mean?* asks someone to explain what they said.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: *Wrong* means incorrect or not right: a wrong answer, the wrong bus, morally wrong. *False* means untrue or fake, and fits claims, statements and some objects (*false teeth*, *a false alarm*).
entries.usage: German *falsch* covers both, but English uses *wrong* in most everyday cases: *You have the wrong number*, *I took the wrong exit*, *What's wrong?*. *False* fits formal statements and fixed phrases (*true or false*, *false advertising*, *a false name*). With a noun, say *the wrong train*; *the false train* sounds strange.
examples: I put the **wrong** date on the invitations, so now I have to text everyone.
Three fire trucks showed up, but it turned out to be a **false** alarm.
The company was fined for making **false** claims about its vitamins.

drill.sentence: We got on the {{wrong}} train and ended up in New Jersey instead of Connecticut.
drill.hint: wrong or false? (not the right one)

mistake.wrong: Sorry, I took a false turn.
mistake.right: Sorry, I took a wrong turn.
mistake.why: German *falsch* is usually *wrong*; *false* means untrue or fake.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: German *sicher* has two English words: *sure* means certain (*I'm sure she'll come*), and *safe* means protected from danger or not dangerous.
entries.usage: *I'm sure* is about your knowledge; *I'm safe* is about danger. *Secure* is closer to *sicher* in technical and financial contexts (*a secure password*, *a secure job*). In speech, *Sure!* also means *of course* or *yes* (*Sure, I can help*).
examples: Are you **sure** you turned off the stove?
Is it **safe** to walk around this neighborhood at night?
The missing hikers were found **safe** after a cold night on the mountain.

drill.sentence: I'm not {{sure}} the restaurant takes reservations, so let's call first.
drill.hint: sure or safe? (certain)

mistake.wrong: I'm safe that I locked the door.
mistake.right: I'm sure that I locked the door.
mistake.why: German *sicher* in the sense of certain is *sure*; *safe* means protected from danger.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: German *Folie* in a presentation is a *slide* in English. A *foil* is a thin metal sheet, mostly *aluminum foil* in the kitchen.
entries.usage: Say *the next slide*, *slide 12* and *a slide deck* (or just *deck*) for a presentation. In the kitchen, Americans say *aluminum foil* or *tin foil*, and *plastic wrap* is the clear film. The clear sheets for old overhead projectors were called *transparencies*.
examples: Can you go back one **slide**? I missed the numbers.
Cover the dish with **foil** and bake it for another twenty minutes.
At the rehearsal dinner, they showed **slides** of the couple as little kids.

drill.sentence: Wrap the leftover pizza in {{foil}} and put it in the fridge.
drill.hint: slide or foil? (thin metal sheet)

mistake.wrong: On the next foil, you can see our sales figures.
mistake.right: On the next slide, you can see our sales figures.
mistake.why: German *Folie* in a presentation is a *slide*; *foil* is thin metal.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: German *Praktikum* is usually an *internship*: a short period of work at a company to gain experience. In the US, a *practicum* is supervised practical training that is part of a degree, mostly in teaching, counseling, nursing or social work.
entries.usage: Americans say *do an internship*, and German *Praktikant* is *intern* (*a summer intern at a law firm*). *Practicum* sounds academic and is used only inside those degree programs. In hospitals, *interns* are first-year doctors, which is a different meaning.
examples: She did a summer **internship** at a newspaper in Atlanta.
Every education student does a semester-long **practicum** in a local school.
We have two **interns** this summer, both college juniors.

drill.sentence: After his sophomore year, he landed a paid {{internship}} at an architecture firm in Philadelphia.
drill.hint: internship or practicum? (work experience at a company)

mistake.wrong: I'm doing a practicum at a car company this summer.
mistake.right: I'm doing an internship at a car company this summer.
mistake.why: German *Praktikum* at a company is an *internship*; a *practicum* is training inside a degree in fields like teaching or nursing.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: German *Mobbing*, repeated attacks on someone at school or work, is *bullying* in English (*workplace bullying*). English *mobbing* usually means a crowd surrounding or attacking someone.
entries.usage: *Bullying* covers insults, threats, exclusion and online attacks (*cyberbullying*), and the person who does it is a *bully*. Most Americans won't understand *mobbing* in the German sense, though it appears in some HR texts. *Be mobbed by fans* or *by reporters* means surrounded by an excited crowd.
examples: The school has a strict policy against **bullying**, including online.
The singer was **mobbed** by fans outside her hotel.
He finally reported his manager for years of **bullying** and humiliation.

drill.sentence: Our son was being {{bullied}} by older kids on the school bus, so we drove him to school for a month.
drill.hint: bullying or mobbing? (repeated cruelty to a weaker person)

mistake.wrong: She left the company because of mobbing by her colleagues.
mistake.right: She left the company because her coworkers were bullying her.
mistake.why: German *Mobbing* is *bullying*; English *mobbing* usually means a crowd surrounding someone.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: German *Fotoshooting* is a *photo shoot* in English. In American English, *a shooting* almost always means an attack with a gun.
entries.usage: Use *photo shoot* or just *shoot* (*a fashion shoot*, *The shoot ran late*). Never say *We had a shooting yesterday* about photos, because it sounds like a crime report. The verb *shoot* is fine for photos and video (*They shot the ad in Utah*).
examples: We booked a **photo shoot** in the park for our engagement pictures.
The **shoot** ran three hours over because of the rain.
They **shot** the whole commercial in one day in the desert.

drill.sentence: The magazine flew the band to Iceland for a two-day {{photo shoot}} on a black-sand beach.
drill.hint: the English for German *Fotoshooting*

mistake.wrong: We had a shooting with a professional photographer last weekend.
mistake.right: We had a photo shoot with a professional photographer last weekend.
mistake.why: In American English, *a shooting* means a gun attack; German *Fotoshooting* is *photo shoot*.

entries.label: false friend
entries.meaning: German *realisieren*, to carry out a plan or project, is usually *implement*, *carry out* or *complete* in English. English *realize* mostly means to suddenly become aware of something.
entries.usage: *We realized the project* sounds like you suddenly understood it. Use *implement* for plans, policies and systems (*implement the new rules*), *carry out* in plainer English, and *build* or *finish* for physical projects. The older sense survives in *realize a dream* and *realize your potential*.
examples: The city will **implement** the new recycling rules in January.
I suddenly **realized** I'd been calling him the wrong name all evening.
It took five years, but they finally **realized** their dream of opening a bookstore.

drill.sentence: The airline needs a few months to {{implement}} the new boarding process at every gate.
drill.hint: implement or realize? (put a plan into action)

mistake.wrong: The team realized the new parking system in only three months.
mistake.right: The team implemented the new parking system in only three months.
mistake.why: German *realisieren* is *implement*, *carry out* or *complete*; English *realize* usually means suddenly understand.

entries.label: US vs. UK
entries.meaning: In the US, the *first floor* is the floor at street level, German *Erdgeschoss*. The floor above it is the *second floor*, while British English says *ground floor* and *first floor*.
entries.usage: So German *erster Stock* is the American *second floor*. Americans also say *ground floor*, especially in *ground-floor apartment* or *ground-floor shops*, but when they count floors, street level is the *first floor*. *Get in on the ground floor* is a fixed phrase meaning *join early*.
examples: Our apartment is on the **first floor**, so we can walk right out to the yard.
Our hotel in London had the lobby on the **ground floor** and our room one flight up, on what they called the first floor.
The restrooms are on the **second floor**, right above the café.

drill.sentence: The lobby and the mailroom are on the {{first floor}}, and the gym is one flight up, on the second.
drill.hint: first floor or ground floor? (US counting: the next floor up is the second)

mistake.wrong: My office is on the first floor, one flight of stairs up.
mistake.right: My office is on the second floor, one flight of stairs up.
mistake.why: In the US, street level is the *first floor*, so one floor up is the *second floor*.

entries.label: preposition
entries.meaning: In English, people and things are *in* a picture, photo or painting. German *auf dem Bild* leads to *on the picture*, which natives hear as physically on top of it.
entries.usage: Say *Who's that in the photo?* and *the woman in the painting*. *On* is for the surface itself (*There's a coffee stain on the photo*) and for screens and pages (*on the screen*, *on page 5*). *In the picture* can also mean part of someone's life or a situation (*Is her ex still in the picture?*).
examples: Who's the little girl **in this picture**? Is that you?
**In the photo**, my parents are standing in front of their first car.
There's a dog **in** almost every painting she makes.

drill.sentence: That's me {{in}} the photo, the kid with the red hat and the missing tooth.
drill.hint: in or on? (German *auf dem Bild*)

mistake.wrong: Who is the woman on the picture?
mistake.right: Who is the woman in the picture?
mistake.why: People and things shown in an image are *in* it; *on* refers to its surface.

entries.label: uncountable noun
entries.meaning: *Furniture* is uncountable in English: no plural and no *a*. For one item, say *a piece of furniture* or name the item (*a table*, *a couch*).
entries.usage: Say *some furniture*, *a lot of furniture*, *new furniture*, and use a singular verb (*The furniture is old*). German *Möbel* is plural, which leads to *furnitures* and *the furniture are*. A *furnished* apartment comes with furniture.
examples: We sold most of our **furniture** before moving to Hawaii.
This chair is the only **piece of furniture** I kept from my first apartment.
The **furniture** in the lobby is old but really comfortable.

drill.sentence: We need to buy some new {{furniture}} for the living room before my in-laws visit.
drill.hint: the uncountable word for tables, chairs and beds

mistake.wrong: All the furnitures are included in the rent.
mistake.right: All the furniture is included in the rent.
mistake.why: *Furniture* is uncountable, so it has no plural and takes a singular verb.

entries.label: uncountable noun
entries.meaning: *Equipment* is uncountable: it has no plural and does not take *a*. For one item, say *a piece of equipment* or name the item.
entries.usage: Say *camping equipment*, *medical equipment* and *a lot of equipment*, with a singular verb (*The equipment is expensive*). In speech, *gear* is a common casual alternative (*hiking gear*). The verb *equip* takes *with*: *The kitchen is equipped with a dishwasher*.
examples: The gym has great **equipment**, but it's always crowded after work.
Hospitals need backup power for their **equipment** during storms.
New lab members get safety training before they use any **equipment**.

drill.sentence: We rented all our camping {{equipment}}, so we only had to bring food and clothes.
drill.hint: the uncountable word for tents, stoves and other tools (not *gear*)

mistake.wrong: We bought new equipments for the kitchen.
mistake.right: We bought new equipment for the kitchen.
mistake.why: *Equipment* is uncountable, so it never takes a plural *-s*.

entries.label: uncountable noun
entries.meaning: *Software* is uncountable: no plural and no *a*. To count it, say *a software package*, *a program*, *an app* or *a tool*.
entries.usage: Say *some software*, *a lot of software* and *software tools*, with a singular verb (*The software is out of date*). In speech, *app* and *program* are more common for one product (*Which app do you use?*). *Hardware* follows the same rule.
examples: Our accountant uses special **software** to prepare tax returns.
The **software** on our old TV hasn't been updated in years.
The school bought new reading **software** for its first graders.

drill.sentence: My laptop is so old that it can't run the latest {{software}} anymore.
drill.hint: the uncountable word for programs

mistake.wrong: We compared three different softwares for our team.
mistake.right: We compared three different software tools for our team.
mistake.why: *Software* is uncountable; to count products, say *programs*, *tools* or *apps*.

entries.term: Do you know where it is? (not 'where is it')
entries.spoken_term: Do you know where it is?
entries.label: word order
entries.meaning: After *Do you know*, *Can you tell me* and *I wonder*, a question becomes an indirect question with statement word order: *where it is*, not *where is it*.
entries.usage: The subject comes before the verb, and *do* or *did* disappears: *Do you know what time it starts?*, not *what time does it start*. Indirect questions sound more polite, so they are common with strangers and in emails. Without a question word, use *if* or *whether*: *Do you know if the store is open?*
entries.pattern: Do you know / Can you tell me + question word + subject + verb
examples: **Do you know where** I **put** my car keys? I had them a minute ago.
Can you tell me **what time the museum closes**?
I wonder **why she left** the party so early.

drill.sentence: Do you know {{where the bus stop is}}? I'm trying to get downtown.
drill.hint: Rewrite as an indirect question: Where is the bus stop?

mistake.wrong: Do you know where is the train station?
mistake.right: Do you know where the train station is?
mistake.why: In indirect questions, the subject comes before the verb.

entries.term: What do you call …? (not 'How do you call …?')
entries.spoken_term: What do you call this in English?
entries.label: question form
entries.meaning: To ask for the name of something, English uses *What do you call…?*. German *Wie nennt man…?* leads to *How do you call…?*, which is wrong in this sense.
entries.usage: Use *What do you call this in English?* or *What's this called?* to ask for a name, and *How do you say … in English?* to ask for a translation. *How do you call someone?* is a real question, but it asks how to reach them by phone.
examples: **What do you call** the little plastic tip on a shoelace?
**What's** this kind of pasta **called**? It looks like little ears.
**How do you say** "thank you" in Korean?

drill.sentence: {{What do you call}} a baby kangaroo? I can never remember.
drill.hint: ask for the name of something (not *How …*)

mistake.wrong: How do you call this in English?
mistake.right: What do you call this in English?
mistake.why: To ask for a name, use *What do you call…?*; *how* goes with *say*.

entries.label: question form
entries.meaning: *What's she like?* asks about someone's personality or character. *How is she?* asks about her health or how she is doing right now.
entries.usage: German *Wie ist sie?* covers both, but *How is she?* usually asks whether she is well or how she is feeling. *What's … like?* also works for places and things: *What's Seattle like?*, *What was the food like?*. *What does she look like?* asks only about appearance.
examples: "I'm meeting Daniel's sister tomorrow. **What's she like**?" "Really funny. You'll love her."
**What's** the weather **like** in Phoenix in March?
"**How is she**?" "Much better, thanks. She's home from the hospital."

drill.sentence: "Your new roommate moved in? {{What's she like}}?" "Quiet, neat and a really good cook."
drill.hint: ask about her personality (not *How is she?*)

mistake.wrong: I haven't met your brother yet. How is he?
mistake.right: I haven't met your brother yet. What's he like?
mistake.why: *How is he?* asks about health or mood; to ask about someone's character, say *What's he like?*.

entries.label: preposition
entries.meaning: *The same* is followed by *as*: *the same as yours*, *the same color as the sky*. German *das gleiche wie* leads to *the same like*, which is wrong.
entries.usage: Other comparison words have fixed prepositions too: *similar to*, *different from* (in the US also *different than*), and *like* alone before a noun (*It looks like mine*). *Same* almost always takes *the*: *I have the same problem*. In casual speech, *Same here* or just *Same* means *me too*.
examples: My phone is **the same as** yours, but it's a different color.
We ordered **the same** pizza **as** last time.
Her new apartment is about **the same** size **as** ours.

drill.sentence: Your backpack is exactly {{the same as}} the one my son carries to school.
drill.hint: identical to (German *das gleiche wie*)

mistake.wrong: Your car is the same like mine.
mistake.right: Your car is the same as mine.
mistake.why: *The same* is followed by *as*, not *like*.

entries.label: time expression
entries.meaning: *Lately* and *recently* mean *in the recent period up to now*, German *in letzter Zeit*. *The last time* means the most recent single occasion (*The last time I saw her, she was moving*).
entries.usage: German *in letzter Zeit* is *lately* or *recently*; *in the last time* is not English. *Lately* goes with the present perfect, often at the end of the clause, while *recently* also works with the simple past for one event (*I recently moved*). *These days* and *in recent weeks* are other natural options.
examples: My knee has been bothering me a lot **lately**, so I skipped the race.
Is it just me, or has it been really windy **lately**?
Prices at the farmers market have gone up a lot **lately**.

drill.sentence: I haven't been to the gym much {{lately}}; work has been crazy.
drill.hint: *in letzter Zeit*, one word, often at the end (not *recently*)

mistake.wrong: In the last time I've been very tired.
mistake.right: I've been very tired lately.
mistake.why: German *in letzter Zeit* is *lately* or *recently*; *the last time* means the most recent occasion.

entries.label: time expression
entries.meaning: English uses *this* for parts of the current day (*this morning*, *this afternoon*, *this evening*) and *last night* for the night before. German *heute Morgen* leads to *today morning*, which is wrong.
entries.usage: Use *yesterday morning*, *yesterday afternoon* and *yesterday evening*, but *last night* is far more natural than *yesterday night*. *Tonight* means this evening or the coming night. For the next day, *tomorrow morning* and *tomorrow night* are correct.
examples: I saw a deer in our backyard **this morning**.
We stayed up way too late **last night** playing board games.
Are you free **this afternoon** for a quick call?

drill.sentence: I'm so tired. The neighbors' party went on until 3 a.m. {{last night}}.
drill.hint: *gestern Nacht* in natural English (not *yesterday …*)

mistake.wrong: I called you today morning, but you didn't answer.
mistake.right: I called you this morning, but you didn't answer.
mistake.why: English says *this morning*; *today morning* is a word-for-word translation.

entries.label: collocation
entries.meaning: In English, you *take* a class or a course. German *einen Kurs besuchen* leads to *visit a course*, which sounds like you went to look at it once.
entries.usage: Americans usually say *class* for one course (*I'm taking a yoga class*), while *course* sounds more formal or academic. *Attend a class* is correct but formal and is about being physically there. *Sign up for* or *enroll in* a class means you registered.
examples: I'm **taking** a pottery **class** with my mom this spring.
She **took** an online **course** in bookkeeping before starting her business.
Have you ever **taken** a dance **class**?

drill.sentence: This semester I'm {{taking}} four classes and working twenty hours a week, so I barely sleep.
drill.hint: visit, attend or take? (your course load for the semester)

mistake.wrong: Last year I visited a course in photography.
mistake.right: Last year I took a course in photography.
mistake.why: German *einen Kurs besuchen* is *take a course*; *visit* means go to see a place or a person.

entries.label: collocation
entries.meaning: Americans *make* a decision. *Take a decision* is correct in British English, especially in formal and business contexts, but it sounds foreign to most Americans.
entries.usage: German *eine Entscheidung treffen* has no word-for-word match: use *make a decision*, or simply *decide*, which is often more natural (*We decided to wait*). Common combinations are *make a tough decision*, *make the right decision* and *a decision was made*.
examples: We have to **make a decision** about the apartment by the end of the week.
We **made** the **decision** to move closer to my parents last spring.
The referee **made** a terrible **decision** in the last minute of the game.

drill.sentence: Stop worrying about it tonight. Sleep on it, and {{make}} a decision in the morning.
drill.hint: make or take? (the American verb with *a decision*)

mistake.wrong: We took the decision to sell the house.
mistake.right: We made the decision to sell the house.
mistake.why: *Take a decision* is British; Americans *make* a decision.

entries.label: preposition
entries.meaning: In English, information and people are *on* the internet, *on* a website and *online*. German *im Internet* leads to *in the internet*, which is wrong.
entries.usage: Say *I found it on the internet*, *on Google*, *on YouTube*, *on social media* and *on the web*. *Online* alone is common and casual (*I bought it online*). Modern American style writes *internet* with a small *i*.
examples: I found the manual for our old dishwasher **on the internet**.
Don't believe everything you read **online**.
My grandma posts photos of her garden **on** Facebook every morning.

drill.sentence: I looked up my symptoms {{on}} the internet and immediately started to panic.
drill.hint: in or on? (German *im Internet*)

mistake.wrong: I read it in the internet.
mistake.right: I read it on the internet.
mistake.why: English uses *on* with *the internet*, websites and social media.

entries.label: preposition
entries.meaning: *Depend* is followed by *on* (or formally *upon*): *It depends on the weather*. German *abhängen von* leads to *depend of* or *depend from*, which are wrong.
entries.usage: *It depends* can stand alone as a full answer, and *It depends on whether…* and *It depends on how…* are common. The adjective *dependent* also takes *on*, but *independent* usually takes *of*: *independent of the results*.
examples: Whether I can come **depends on** when my shift ends.
"Are you coming tonight?" "It **depends**. Do I have to bring anything?"
Many small beach towns **depend on** tourism for most of their income.

drill.sentence: The price of the trip {{depends on}} how many people sign up.
drill.hint: German *hängt … ab von*: the verb + the right preposition

mistake.wrong: It depends of the price.
mistake.right: It depends on the price.
mistake.why: *Depend* takes *on*; German *von* is not *of* here.

entries.label: preposition
entries.meaning: In English, you have *a question for* someone, or you *ask* someone a question. German *eine Frage an dich* leads to *a question to you*, which sounds unnatural.
entries.usage: Say *I have a question for you* and *Can I ask you something?*, with no *to* after *ask*. *Put a question to* someone exists, but it is formal and typical of debates and interviews. *Question* as a verb means doubt or interrogate (*The police questioned him*).
examples: I have a quick **question for you** about the parking situation.
My son **asked** his teacher a **question** she couldn't answer.
The reporters had lots of **questions for** the fire chief.

drill.sentence: Before you go, I have one more {{question for}} you about Saturday's trip.
drill.hint: the noun + the right preposition (German *Frage an*)

mistake.wrong: I have a question to you.
mistake.right: I have a question for you.
mistake.why: With *question*, English uses *for* the person; German *an* is not *to* here.

entries.label: usage trap
entries.meaning: *Almost* is an adverb, so it cannot go directly before a plain noun. Use it with *all*, *every-* words and *no-* words: *almost everyone*, *almost all people*, *almost nobody*.
entries.usage: German *fast alle* is *almost all* or *almost everyone*; *almost people* and *almost students* are wrong. *Most* means the majority (*most people*), and *most of* comes before *the*, *my* or a pronoun (*most of the students*). *Almost* also goes with numbers and verbs: *almost 200 guests*, *I almost missed the bus*.
examples: **Almost everyone** in the office got the flu last winter.
**Almost all** my friends from college have moved out of the city.
**Almost nobody** in our town takes the bus; everyone drives.

drill.sentence: {{Almost everyone}} I invited came to the party, even my cousin from Alaska.
drill.hint: *fast alle*: two words, not *nearly …* and not *almost people*

mistake.wrong: Almost people in my town have a car.
mistake.right: Almost everyone in my town has a car.
mistake.why: *Almost* cannot go directly before a noun; use *almost everyone*, *almost all people* or *most people*.

entries.label: US vs. UK
entries.meaning: Americans say *on the weekend* for one weekend and *on weekends* for weekends in general. *At the weekend* is British.
entries.usage: Germans who learned British English at school often say *at the weekend*, which Americans understand but notice as British. *This weekend*, *next weekend* and *last weekend* take no preposition. *Over the weekend* means during the weekend (*I'll read it over the weekend*).
examples: We usually go hiking **on the weekend** if the weather's nice.
The farmers market downtown is only open **on weekends** from May to October.
We drove up to the mountains **over the weekend** to see the fall colors.

drill.sentence: My brother works at a restaurant, so he's almost never free {{on}} weekends.
drill.hint: on or at? (US)

mistake.wrong: What did you do at the weekend?
mistake.right: What did you do on the weekend?
mistake.why: *At the weekend* is British; Americans say *on the weekend*, *over the weekend* or *last weekend*.

entries.label: preposition
entries.meaning: *Across from* means on the other side of a street, room or table, facing something, like German *gegenüber*. *In front of* means directly before something on the same side, like German *vor*.
entries.usage: *The bank is in front of the hotel* means it stands between the hotel and the street; for the other side of the street, say *across from* (US) or *opposite* (more British and formal). At a table, *She sat across from me* means she faced you. *Across the street* works without *from*: *They live across the street*.
examples: There's a great coffee shop right **across from** our office.
At dinner, I sat **across from** a woman who had lived in Kenya for ten years.
Someone parked **in front of** our driveway, so I couldn't get out.

drill.sentence: The pharmacy is {{across from}} the post office, on the other side of Elm Street.
drill.hint: in front of or across from? (German *gegenüber*)

mistake.wrong: The bus stop is in front of the bank, on the other side of the street.
mistake.right: The bus stop is across from the bank, on the other side of the street.
mistake.why: German *gegenüber* is *across from* or *opposite*; *in front of* means directly before it on the same side.
